Except that the phone in question is a 5c, which doesn't have a secure enclave...

Okay; so following the breadcrumbs from the Daily Beast article to the trailofbits article, it looks like the 5c has an architecture that is similar to how a smart card works.

That is; there's a little "Secure Enclave" cpu, that is separate from the iPhone cpu, which has it's own firmware, which is never updated. The SE contains the private key, and that can only be accessed (not copied) by giving the SE the PIN, through the SE's API which manages brute-force PIN retries via a physical delay. (assuming you can't feed the SE bogus clock data to speed up these delays). This inaccessible private key is used to encrypt the secret (symmetric) key, which is used to encrypt the user's data store.

I can see a few different ways around this. 1. MAYBE you can feed the SE a bogus clock signal, so you can overcome the PIN retry timer, and use that to brute-force the PIN. (unless the SE has it's own clock - and if it does, there are probably ways to fuck with that which don't involve direct API calls: Smart Cards have been attacked at the physical level. 2. MAYBE you can clone the SE, and then also, the phone, and run it in a virtualized environment. Brute force the PIN; and every time, re-set the VM, so that the phone does not know it's a retry. (let's assume that the SE is designed to prevent cloning, just like Smart Cards presumably are).

In both cases, I don't see why the FBI needs Apple to do this.

But I DO see why Apple is fighting back. They do not want to support the legal precedent. This could become a huge deal. It would also undermine the technology behind smart cards.
